analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration in car sale and lease contracts unless the buyer agrees to arbitrate after a dispute arises.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House Judiciary subcommittee by voice vote in July 2008 but never received a full committee vote or a floor vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly every car sale or lease contract today includes a clause requiring disputes to be settled by a private arbitrator rather than a court, decided before the buyer ever has a problem. This bill would change that for motor vehicle contracts: arbitration would be allowed only if, after a dispute actually arises, both the buyer and the dealer agree in writing to arbitrate. It would also require arbitrators to briefly explain the basis for their decisions. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, approved by a subcommittee without opposition, and then never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers and lessees. Today, a nearly universal contract clause requires disputes with a dealer to go to a private arbitrator whose decisions are largely unappealable and whose reasoning may never be explained. The bill would let a buyer take a dealer to court unless the buyer voluntarily agrees to arbitration after a problem comes up, and would require a written explanation of any award on request.

how_it_helps.text: It bars settlement of car sale or lease disputes by arbitration unless all parties agree in writing after the dispute has actually arisen, so a dealer can no longer rely on a clause signed before a problem occurred.
It requires an arbitration award, at a party's request, to include a brief, informal discussion of the factual and legal basis for the decision, so consumers can understand and challenge a ruling.

analysis.who_pays: Auto dealers and arbitration providers would bear the cost. Dealers would lose the advantage of forcing every dispute into a forum they help choose, and arbitration firms would lose the steady stream of cases those clauses supply. Some disputes would cost more to resolve in court, and dealers argue litigation is slower for small claims.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is often faster and cheaper than going to court, and some buyers with small-dollar disputes might prefer it; the bill's required written explanation of awards adds a layer of process that its backers would have to pay for.
The bill would push more car disputes into the court system, raising costs for dealers and potentially increasing the volume of small claims litigation that courts and dealers would have to absorb.
The bill applies only to contracts entered into, amended, or renewed after enactment, so buyers locked into existing contracts with mandatory arbitration clauses would get no relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it would restore the right of a car buyer to take a dealer to court instead of being forced into a private arbitration process with no appeal and no written explanation. The main costs are acknowledged and modest: dealers and arbitration firms would face more litigation, cases might be slower or more expensive for a few very small disputes, and arbitration would still be available whenever both sides agree to it after a problem arises. On balance, the consumer protections outweigh the costs, and the bill had cleared a subcommittee without recorded opposition. Its main flaw was that it never reached the full committee or the floor.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee approved it by voice vote in July 2008, but the full Judiciary Committee never took it up and no floor vote ever happened, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced February 7, 2008 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On February 29, 2008 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on March 6, 2008.
On July 15, 2008 the subcommittee held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote.
No further action was ever recorded: the full committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill, which died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automobile dealers and arbitration providers kept the status quo: car buyers remain bound by arbitration clauses they signed before any dispute, and cases stay out of court.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill advanced only as far as a Democratic-controlled subcommittee, which approved it by voice vote; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: Dealers sell and lease cars with contracts containing mandatory arbitration clauses, which let disputes be decided privately rather than in court; the bill would void those clauses' advance effect, forcing dealers to face buyers' lawsuits unless the buyer agrees to arbitration after a dispute. For ordinary buyers, this restores access to court, which is why the dealers' interest runs against the public's in this bill.

Companies that administer consumer arbitrations depend on contracts signed before a dispute, which guarantee a stream of cases; the bill would cut off the automatic supply of auto cases and require post-dispute consent. Arbitration was already open to any consumer who wanted it, so the industry's position here runs against the public's.
